title: Unnamed celebrity accused of 'inappropriate sexual activities', court hears
excerpt: A two-day trial is being held at the High Court in London
description: A two-day trial is being held at the High Court in London
content:
A two-day trial is being held at the High Court in London

A celebrity has asked the High Court to prevent two news organisations from publishing his identity and allegations that he abused his status for many years to engage, or attempt to engage, in "inappropriate sexual activities with a large number of girls and young women".

---

### 📰 The Full Developing Story & Context

The unnamed celebrity is seeking an injunction, and his legal team told the first day of a trial on Tuesday that any publication would be "highly likely" to lead him to kill himself.

They told the court that his drastic reaction was not because of any wrongdoing, but because of the fear of "trial by media".

The man denies abusing "his power and position as a celebrity to contact and forge relationships with young women and teenagers to try to have sex with them", the court heard.

The legal team for ITN and Guardian News and Media (GNM) told the court that the celebrity's "suicide risk" could be mitigated and there was no proper basis "to restrain the publication of public interest journalism".

A medical report carried out for the court said inpatient treatment could provide "significant, but not complete mitigation of the risk", but that treatment, perhaps for months, had "a realistic potential to reduce the risk".

The judge, Mr Justice Nicklin, said there was "significant public interest" in the proceedings and that "this is a difficult and important case".

He added: "The court must determine it fairly, on the evidence and legal submissions."

Nicklin will not determine the truth or accuracy of the allegations, only whether they can be published.

He also urged the press and public not to speculate about the identity of the man, who is referred to in court as PPT.

"The existence of online speculation, however confidently expressed or widely repeated, does not authorise anyone to identify, or purport authoritatively to identify, PPT in connection with these proceedings," he said.

"Nor does repetition transform speculation into established fact."

Sara Mansoori KC, representing the man, told the court that any publication "would have a potentially fatal impact".

The barrister told the court: "The only reason they would not be fatal is because the claimant would be locked up and prevented from his desire to end his life."

---

### 🔍 Background, Statements & Official Perspectives

She said the man had made a suicide attempt after receiving letters from ITN and GNM asking for his response to the allegations, and later absconded from hospital and attempted suicide for a second time.

She added in written submissions: "This is not a case where an individual has spuriously raised 'mental health' concerns in the face of an impending publication that they do not wish to occur.

"The claimant has attempted suicide twice as a result of these matters, been hospitalised for months, been the subject of involuntary detention and been examined by multiple - now more than 10 - doctors."

Mansoori also said the man "has no intention of returning to public life".

Gavin Millar KC, for ITN and GNM, said in written submissions that "numerous allegations" had been gathered during "a wide-ranging and rigorous investigation" and that there was a "strong" public interest in publishing them.

He said reporters had spoken to more than 100 people, and that the resulting allegations "indicated a pattern of behaviour".

Millar later said many of the women "have been traumatised by the claimant's alleged conduct and have suffered mental health crises and mental illness as a result".



---

### 🎙️ Perspectives & What Comes Next

He added that while the state may have a responsibility to protect life, applying that principle to this case would require the state to intervene in "lawful journalistic activities" to prevent "an autonomous act by the claimant himself".

The BBC Action Line website has information about organisations that can offer support for the issues raised in this story.

title: Netherlands pulls out of Eurovision again over Israel participation
excerpt: Claude Kiambe was the last Netherlands entrant in 2025
description: Claude Kiambe was the last Netherlands entrant in 2025
content:
Claude Kiambe was the last Netherlands entrant in 2025

The Netherlands has pulled out of next year's Eurovision Song Contest, with public broadcaster NPO citing "sensitivities" over Israel's participation - reversing a previous decision to take part.

---

### 📰 The Full Developing Story & Context

The Netherlands and four other countries boycotted this year's event, after Dutch network Avrotros pulled out.

Avrotros said it would also not take part next year, but NPO, which oversees public broadcasting in the country, stepped in and pledged last month that the country would return in 2027.

However, NPO's media director Jurre Bosman said on Tuesday that "Israel's participation elicits various reactions in society and causes discussion and division", and NPO "has decided to forgo participation in 2027".

NPO chair Jet de Ranitz said the organisation had held discussions with broadcasters about participating next year.

"In those discussions, we initially felt there was sufficient support to return. Unfortunately, we were unable to find a suitable format for this.

"As a result, we must conclude that it is currently too early to participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027.

"Due to the sensitivities surrounding the themes currently at play, we have decided to take a step back for the time being."

NPO acknowledged that some Dutch fans may be disappointed, but that the contest would still be aired in the Netherlands.

Eurovision Song Contest director Martin Green said he was "deeply sorry" that the Netherlands would not take part, but added that "we understand their decision, and we respect the strength of feeling behind it".

Green added that organisers recognise that opinions about the contest "differ widely, both within countries and between them", adding: "We do not dismiss any of those views.

"At the same time, we believe the Eurovision Song Contest matters in a divided world. It is one of the few moments each year when people from across Europe and beyond come together around music, creativity and shared experience.

"That spirit of unity is what the contest has always stood for, and we are committed to protecting it."

Green said they looked forward to welcoming a Dutch entry again when they "feel the time is right".

---

### 🔍 Background, Statements & Official Perspectives

The Netherlands, Iceland, Spain, Ireland and Slovenia all bocotted the 2026 contest over Israel's participation, amid criticism of its military actions in Gaza and the Middle East.

Eurovision organisers have announced a number of changes in an attempt to address the divisions, including to exclude any country involved in an armed conflict from hosting the competition, and changes to the voting.

As well as the Netherlands, Ireland will also not take part in 2027, and the head of the Spanish public broadcaster has come out in favour of a boycott.

The Czech public broadcaster has also pulled out, but cited spending cuts as the reason.

Eurovision 2027 will take place in Burgas in Bulgaria on 15 May, following Dara's win in Vienna this year with the dance track Bangaranga.

title: Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing
excerpt: Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing
description: Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing
content:
Big, noisy and coming to a town near you - why the data centre backlash is growing

Until a few years ago many of us may have been blissfully unaware of what a data centre was.

---

### 📰 The Full Developing Story & Context

These giant, warehouse-like buildings power virtually all our internet activity, from our web searches and emails to movie downloads and online banking.

They are at the heart of the AI boom, housing the advanced computer chips and servers needed to run services like ChatGPT and Claude.

But the speed at which they're growing, the enormous amount of electricity they consume and concerns about their environmental impact are fuelling a public backlash around the world.

In the US, they've become a huge issue ahead of the midterm elections on 3 November, with both Republicans and opposition Democrats coming out against their development.

It's putting opponents of data centre expansion on a collision course with US President Donald Trump, who has dismissed the pushback as a "sick conspiracy", even as public anger grows.

Here's what you need to know about the data centre boom, and why opposition is growing.

There are about 12,250 data centres around the world, according to Data Center Map, external, a company that tracks both operational and pre-operational sites.

That's up sharply from 2021, when there were around 8,000, external operational sites.

As the chart below shows, data centres are most densely clustered in the US which has 4,767 sites. It is followed by Europe, where the UK and Germany lead.

Data centres have typically been located near to cities where it's easier to access high voltage power lines or water resources for cooling. But as they get bigger, more are being built in rural areas.

But when it comes to actual capacity, the US is ahead by a much larger margin, with China in second place and Europe lagging far behind.

This gap is set to widen in the coming years, leading some to warn Europe risks missing out on the potential economic benefits of the AI boom, external.

Data centres vary wildly in size, ranging from ones that fit inside a garden shed to others covering vast expanses of land.

The world's largest operational data centre is widely reported to be one run by China Telecom in Hohhot, Inner Mongolia, covering an area of approximately one million square metres (10.7 million sq ft). That is equivalent to about 140 Fifa football pitches.

However, much larger sites are under construction as the graphic below shows.

All these sites are being built exclusively to provide the immense computing power needed to run AI services.

For instance, Colossus 2, which is part of the wider Colossus campus, will house hundreds of thousands of advanced AI chips made by tech giant Nvidia.

It will also be used to train xAI's chatbot Grok. Elon Musk's company will use 41 methane gas turbines to help power the site, which activists say could "significantly increase" local air pollution, external. Local regulators say the turbines will meet air quality standards.

The pressure data centres put on local resources has sparked increasing concern. These facilities can use significant amounts of water to cool their systems, which could lead to water shortages, some experts say.

Data centres worldwide are also thought to consume more electricity than the whole of France, as the chart below shows.

This growing hunger for power is driving up carbon emissions, analysis shows, while putting pressure on local grids, which some fear could push up energy prices.

With others worried about the noise data centres make and the space they take up, a public backlash is gathering steam.

---

### 🔍 Background, Statements & Official Perspectives

Some 16 US states have proposed laws to ban or temporarily block new facilities, and it could be a key issue in November's midterm elections.

Outside the US, opposition to data centres has emerged in countries like Mexico, France, Indonesia and the UK.

But supporters say data centres are critical to national security, and the development of AI.

They also say they are good for the economy, external, attracting investment, generating tax revenue and creating jobs in areas like construction.

A recent report by the Brookings Center, external suggests data centres do create local jobs, although fewer than industry advocates claim.

The type of data centre matters too. So-called hyperscale facilities - massive sites owned and run by tech giants like Amazon and Microsoft - have a bigger positive effect on jobs, it found.

But "colocation" facilities, which lease space to remote tenants without a local presence, brought fewer benefits.

As the debate over their merits intensifies, the data centre rollout continues.

This year, the tech industry is expected to spend a combined $765bn, external ($544bn) on AI infrastructure in 2026, with this topping $1tn next year.

But as concerns about the environmental impact grow, the tech industry is exploring alternatives.

One idea is to put data centres in space, external or on the Moon, where they could harness abundant solar energy.

Others predict that more AI processing could eventually be carried out by the hardware already inside our computers and smartphones, reducing the need for vast data centres altogether.

description: Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listi...
content:
Anthropic has warned artificial intelligence (AI) could pose "catastrophic or existential risks to humanity" as it unveiled details of its planned blockbuster stock market listing in the US.

The firm's valuation is expected to exceed that of SpaceX, which was the biggest-ever listing at an initial valuation of about $1.8 trillion in the summer.

---

### 📰 The Full Developing Story & Context

Anthropic has not yet disclosed the number of shares to be released, their price range, or a date for the listing.

The Claude chatbot developer reported $16.3bn (£12.2bn) of revenue in the first half of the year, with losses of more than $80.7bn.

Anthropic, which said it will list on the Nasdaq under the symbol ANT, will be the first fully AI-focused company to go public, making it a test case for the future of the technology.

In a filing ahead of its listing, Anthropic said concerns had been raised by policymakers, regulators and researchers as well as by people within its organisation that AI systems posed a significant risk to humanity.

It said advanced AI systems "could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponised, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy".

Anthropic was founded five years ago by chief executive Dario Amodei, his sister Daniela Amodei and five others, and announced its intention to go public in June.

Its main rival, OpenAI, quickly followed suit. That listing is now expected to occur early next year, according to a person familiar with OpenAI's plans.

Those announcements were followed by a wave of cyber-security and other technological breaches involving their AI agents - bots designed to operate somewhat autonomously.

Current and former staff of both companies also warned AI technology was being developed without the ability to protect humanity from possible future harms enacted by AI tools.

As Anthropic revealed its stock debut plans on Monday, the owners of the rights to Elvis Presley's music sued the AI firm accusing it of using hundreds of the rock-and-roll star's songs to train its chatbot Claude.

Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know

In Anthropic's new documents, it reiterated promises it has made in the past to develop AI in a way that is beneficial to people, while at the same time warning investors of its dangers.

Anthropic detailed losses in its financial filings that exceeded its revenue for the first half of the year, but said it would often make forward investments "that may seem irresponsibly large at first glance".

"In general, we will aim to be bold but sane, and to win trust with a track record of successful bets," the tech giant said.

Its success depends largely on its ability to develop the most advanced AI models, Anthropic said, adding, "any failure to do so could adversely affect our business".

Across about 90 pages detailing possible risk factors, Anthropic set out the potential threats to its ability to safely and competitively develop AI.

Anthropic warned it relies on a cluster of cloud computing providers, Taiwanese chipmakers already facing huge demand and data centres concentrated in the US.

It also warned of "regulatory action arising from harms associated with our AI models" - citing concerns over AI being used by children or individuals at risk of suicide - and uncertainty about where and how it might be held liable for actions taken by its systems.

---

### 🔍 Background, Statements & Official Perspectives

However, Anthropic also used the filing to laud the potential benefits of the tech itself, envisioning it unlocking "millions of virtual agents with the ability to revolutionise every area of human endeavour" across a range of fields.

"We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history," the firm said.

Anthropic said AI would also "profoundly accelerate the rate of progress in biology and medicine", potentially finding cures to diseases including cancer and Alzheimer's.

The firm added it could also establish "sustained acceleration in economic growth" by boosting productivity.

Matt Orton, chief market strategist at investment management firm Raymond James Investment, said investors expected to see rapid growth as well as rapid financial losses in Anthropic's finances, so Monday's filing would not come as a surprise.

"Getting the details from this filing, I think will help provide the market with more visibility, because we need to know where its revenue growth is coming from," he told the BBC.

Peter Andersen, founder of Andersen Capital Management, told Reuters that Anthropic's plans to list was "a significant milestone in the development of artificial intelligence".

He added that the outcome of its stock market debut would be "fairly indicative of the sentiment" among investors to continue ploughing cash into AI development.

title: Anthropic's blockbuster share listing - 5 surprising things we now know
excerpt: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has become a key figure in the current AI era.
description: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has become a key figure in the current AI era.
content:
Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has become a key figure in the current AI era.

Artificial intelligence (AI) firm Anthropic just released the required paperwork ahead of its long-anticipated debut on the US stock market.

---

### 📰 The Full Developing Story & Context

The 335-page document included fresh details of how the Claude chatbot owner makes money, what it spends that money on and who it is controlled by.

Anthropic also detailed some of the risks it claimed AI technology poses, including how it could take human lives. That information sat alongside the many purported benefits of the technology.

Here are five key points worth highlighting from the filing.

Every public company has to tell potential investors how things could go wrong.

Anthropic's "risk factors" were unique, also disclosing how the AI technology it is developing could doom humanity as a whole.

"Sufficiently advanced AI systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity," Anthropic said.

It noted that less than a year ago, a hacking group Anthropic believed to be sponsored by China "manipulated" Claude to successfully intrude on a number of institutions, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies and government agencies.

But Anthropic said its success is dependent on its ability to constantly "develop, improve, and deploy the most advanced, capable, and useful AI models".

One of the most significant risks to that ability is Anthropic's access to infrastructure it needs, including computer chips and data centres, to build, train and operate the models that underpin its technology.

Anthropic has yet to disclose a target share price for its stock listing.

The company is widely expected to debut with a market valuation of $2 trillion or more, making it the largest stock listing in history. But the figure will be heavily influenced by its financial performance.

Anthropic lost $80.7bn (£60bn) in the first half of this year, double what it lost across 2025 altogether.

The company's overall revenue was $16.2bn for the six-month period. Revenues are rising rapidly, but the firm has a long way to go before it breaks even.

Troy Hooper, co-head of equity capital markets at Mergermarket, said Anthropic's revenue growth is "exceptional". But investors are "less forgiving" of tech companies promising huge future returns than they were even months ago, he added.

Anthropic's debt picture is also unclear given it has a huge amount of accounting charges related to certain forms of investment.

"As a result, investors do not yet have a clear view of Anthropic's underlying profitability or whether its rate of cash generation is sufficient to support the business as it scales," Hooper added.

Despite losing money, Anthropic has heaps of cash lying about.

At $131.6bn, almost all of its cash in hand is defined as "working capital", meaning it can use the money to fund its operations day-to-day.

Currently, Anthropic has more cash on hand than Meta and Google combined.

Anthropic's costs could rise as it faces fierce competition for top staff and computing power from other AI giants.

The leasing of data centres alone is set to cost the company $321.4bn through agreements struck so far this year.

Hooper said such large costs are expected to grow. Even with this kind of cash, it won't be enough to maintain its business growth.

Any investors in Anthropic "will be paying for future dominance, not present-day economics", he said.

Anthropic sees boundless ways it can sell its technology to customers.

A large portion of its current business comes from just 250 major enterprise customers, which it says have paid it at least $10m in the past year.

---

### 🔍 Background, Statements & Official Perspectives

An even smaller number, just five enterprise customers, make up a quarter of its current business.

Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager of Founder ETF, pointed out that "many top Anthropic customers have no long-term contract".

The company's level of business concentration leaves Anthropic dependent on a small fraction of its paying customers to support its growth, with no guarantee it will continue.

Anthropic also has enterprise relationships with the likes of Google and Amazon, both of which are also investors in the company "and competitors", creating potential business conflicts in the future, Monaghan noted.

Anthropic said its overall enterprise customer base has grown rapidly, going from roughly 1,500 customers last year to almost 12,000 this year.

Part of its growth strategy is offering Claude tools for free before working to "convert these users into paying customers over time".

The strategy has led to Claude seeing "the fastest enterprise adoption of any technology in history", the company claimed.

For all of the risks Anthropic has said AI poses, it also reiterated its claim AI will produce an "extraordinary" amount of good.

"Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier AI while mitigating the most significant risks," the company said.

That mission is defined as: "The responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity."

"We do not pursue projects based on commercial opportunity or research novelty alone; our efforts must advance our mission."

Such hypothetical benefits include progress in healthcare, like the development of bespoke treatments for illnesses and improved disease detection, tailored education and legal advice and making more efficient power grids and batteries.

Decades of scientific progress could be condensed into years, accelerating drug discovery, disease detection, and the delivery of personalised therapy.



---

### 🎙️ Perspectives & What Comes Next

Anthropic said AI could provide individually tailored education and expert financial and legal advice, advance power grids and battery design for greater efficiency and reliability and help the "developing world" build more technological capabilities.

"Ultimately, we believe frontier AI will help drive global economic growth," the company said.

title: NANS National Ex-Officio II, Patience Okoroafo, Raises Alarm Over Alleged Marginalization in Akwa Ibom, Calls for Intervention
excerpt: The Akwa Ibom representative at the National Association of Nigerian Students (NANS) National Executive Council, Comr. Patience Nnyenime Okoroafo, has raised concerns over what she describes as sustained marginalization, exclusion and undermining of her office in the state.
description: The Akwa Ibom representative at the National Association of Nigerian Students (NANS) National Executive Council, Comr. Patience Nnyenime Okoroafo, has raised concerns over what she describes as sustained marginalization, exclusion and undermining of her office in the state.
content:
In a report made public, Okoroafo, who serves as National Ex-Officio II at the NANS National Headquarters, accused the Office of the Special Assistant to the Akwa Ibom State Governor on Students Affairs, Comr. Wisdom Emmanuel, of repeatedly sidelining her despite her position as the state's representative at the national student leadership level.

### Dispute Over Representation and Recognition

According to Okoroafo, she emerged as National Ex-Officio II during the last NANS National Convention, becoming the only Akwa Ibom representative occupying a position at the organisation's National Executive Council.

She maintained that her office carries the responsibility of representing and projecting the interests of Akwa Ibom students within the national student leadership structure.

However, she alleged that since her emergence, her office has not received the recognition and institutional support it deserves.

She specifically questioned the repeated involvement of Comr. Dominic Ernest, her Cross River State counterpart, in student-related engagements and activities within Akwa Ibom State, arguing that such responsibilities should ordinarily fall within her representational mandate.

Okoroafo described the situation as an attempt to undermine her position and diminish the relevance of her office.

### Alleges Gender-Based Discrimination and Lack of Support

The NANS official also expressed concerns that her alleged marginalization may be connected to her gender.

Recounting her experience during the NANS National Convention, she alleged that she faced considerable difficulties as a female candidate seeking to represent Akwa Ibom State at the national level.

She further claimed that although the Special Assistant to the Governor on Students Affairs had indicated that government support would be shared between her and Comr. Dominic Ernest, she eventually received no financial assistance from the office.

According to her, this was unlike the experience of some representatives from other states who allegedly received sponsorship and support from their respective state governments.

Despite the challenges, Okoroafo said she financed her campaign through personal sacrifices and contributions from well-wishers, eventually securing victory and bringing national representation to Akwa Ibom State.

She expressed disappointment that, rather than receiving recognition following her emergence, she had continued to experience what she described as exclusion from important student-related engagements.

### Exclusion from Meeting with ARISE with Renewed Hope Leadership

Another major concern raised in the report was her alleged exclusion from a recent meeting involving frontline student leaders and the leadership of ARISE with Renewed Hope.

The meeting reportedly involved Dr. Wisdom Emmanuel, Engr. Uwem Okoko, Hon. Frank Archibong and the Honourable International Coordinator of ARISE with Renewed Hope.

Okoroafo stated that despite being in Akwa Ibom State when the engagement took place, she was neither invited nor informed about the meeting.

She also alleged that she was not briefed on the discussions or outcomes, despite her position within the NANS national leadership structure.

The controversy was further heightened by a social media explanation reportedly given by Comr. Dominic Ernest, who attributed her absence to a national assignment.

However, Okoroafo disputed that explanation, insisting that she was physically present in Akwa Ibom State on the day of the meeting.

She said the discrepancy raises questions about the circumstances surrounding her exclusion and the accuracy of statements made on her behalf.

### Addresses Allegations Concerning Dominic Ernest's Studentship

Meanwhile, Okoroafo also addressed the ongoing controversy surrounding claims circulating online about the studentship status of NANS Vice President, Special Duties, Comr. Dominic Ernest.

She stated that, to the best of her knowledge, Ernest contested the recently concluded NANS National Convention as a student of Cross River State University of Education, Akamkpa.

However, she clarified that determining or declaring his current studentship status was not within her responsibility.

Her position, therefore, was limited to the information available to her regarding his participation in the convention.

### Calls on NANS Leadership and Akwa Ibom Government to Intervene

In her appeal, Okoroafo called on the NANS National Secretariat, the Senate President of NANS, relevant authorities and other stakeholders to intervene and address what she described as the continued marginalization of her office.

She emphasized that her mandate was obtained through the votes of Nigerian students and should be respected irrespective of her gender.

She also appealed for fairness, equity, justice and inclusion within the student leadership structure.

The report was copied to Governor Umo Eno, the NANS National Global President, the NANS Senate President, the Akwa Ibom State Commissioner for Education, security agencies, NANS Zone B leadership and other relevant student leaders.

### The Bigger Question: Representation and Inclusion in Student Leadership

The controversy has brought renewed attention to questions surrounding representation, institutional recognition and inclusion within student leadership structures.

At the centre of the dispute is a fundamental question: Should an elected or conventionally selected representative be excluded from engagements relating to the interests of the constituency they represent?

As the concerns raised by Okoroafo come to public attention, clarification from the offices and individuals mentioned in the report would be important in establishing the full circumstances surrounding the allegations.

For now, Comr. Patience Nnyenime Okoroafo says she remains committed to representing Akwa Ibom students and Nigerian students at large.

**"Aluta Continua! Victoria Ascerta!!"**

*This report is based on a statement issued by Comr. Patience Nnyenime Okoroafo. The allegations contained therein represent her account of events and have not been independently verified. Responses from the individuals and offices mentioned were not included in the statement.*

**Source:** Statement by Comr. Patience Nnyenime Okoroafo, National Ex-Officio II, NANS National Headquarters.

Niger Delta, Nigeria: The Niger Delta Youth Network (NDYN) has unveiled its National Executive Council, comprising young leaders entrusted with the responsibility of advancing the network’s vision, mission, unity, development and collective interests of youths across the Niger Delta region.

The newly constituted National Executive Council is expected to provide strategic leadership and direction as the organization works towards strengthening youth participation in development, promoting peace and unity, and creating opportunities for young people across the region.

Operating under the core values of CONNECT • EMPOWER • TRANSFORM, the NDYN leadership is committed to promoting youth leadership, peacebuilding, entrepreneurship, education, innovation, inclusion, responsible citizenship and sustainable development.

A New Commitment to Niger Delta Youths

According to the network, the National Executive Council will work collectively to strengthen youth engagement and create an environment where young people can contribute meaningfully to the social and economic development of the Niger Delta.

The leadership's focus areas include youth empowerment, entrepreneurship, education, technology and innovation, peace and conflict resolution, stakeholder engagement, gender inclusion, student affairs and sustainable development.

With a broad representation across different areas of youth development and advocacy, the council is expected to leverage collaboration and collective action in addressing issues affecting young people in the region.

Building a Stronger Niger Delta

The NDYN says its ultimate goal is to build a stronger, more united and prosperous Niger Delta where young people are empowered to become leaders, entrepreneurs, innovators and nation builders.

The network's message to Niger Delta youths is clear:

“A Stronger Niger Delta Youths for a Greater Tomorrow.”

With CONNECT • EMPOWER • TRANSFORM serving as its guiding principle, the Niger Delta Youth Network says it is committed to building a platform where young people can connect with one another, access opportunities, develop their capacities and contribute to the future of the region.
